claims.claim: The Chicago Defender was founded in Chicago by Robert S. Abbott on May 5, 1905.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on date.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Chicago dates the founding to May 5, 1905; BPM-003 carries the founding date as verified.
claims.notes: Brief section: FOUNDATION.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago (Chicago History Museum); CTL-DR-BPM-003 research package (verified).

claims.claim: The Defender's first run was about 300 copies, financed by Abbott's own minimal capital (reported as a 25-cent investment).
claims.contradictory_evidence: The precise 25-cent figure is anecdotal and widely repeated; treat the exact number as narrative tradition rather than audited fact.
claims.evidence: Congress (2005) reports about 300 first-run copies. BPM-003 verifies minimal founder capital.
claims.notes: Do not convert the 25-cent tradition into an audited figure. Brief section: CAPITALIZATION.
claims.source: Congressional Record centennial statement (2005); Washington Post retrospective; CTL-DR-BPM-003 (verified minimal founder capital).
claims.source_type: government record; journalism; prior CTL research

claims.claim: The Defender reached about 250,000 weekly circulation by 1929, making it one of the largest-circulation Black newspapers in the United States.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Pre-1940 figures are publisher-claim-era numbers; BPM-003 cautions that pre-1940 circulation figures are approximate.
claims.evidence: Congress's 2005 statement reports more than 250,000 weekly sales by 1929. BPM-003's ledger carries the 1929 and 1945 figures as verified.
claims.notes: Comparative 'largest' framing is conventional but circulation surveys of all Black weeklies are incomplete; carry as comparative language with caution. Brief sections: CIRCULATION.
claims.source: Congressional Record, 2005 centennial statement; CTL-DR-BPM-003 (carries ~250,000 in 1929 and 257,000 in 1945 as verified within that package).

claims.claim: Pullman porters distributed the Defender across the South via the rail network, overcoming Southern bans and local distribution hostility.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on the mechanism; the economics (commissions, bundle costs, losses) are UNRESOLVED (C19).
claims.evidence: BPM-003 carries the porter distribution network as verified; corroborated by congressional and institutional accounts.
claims.notes: This is a distribution mechanism claim, not an economics claim — do not impute margins. Brief section: DISTRIBUTION.
claims.source: CTL-DR-BPM-003 (verified); institutional and congressional histories.

claims.claim: The Defender converted from weekly to daily on February 6, 1956; the print edition ended in 2019 and the paper went online-only.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on the 1956 conversion or 2019 end; exact final print date not confirmed.
claims.evidence: WTTW's July 11, 2019 segment is titled 'Chicago Defender Ends 114-Year Print Run, Goes Online Only.'
claims.notes: Brief section: DECLINE.
claims.source: Wikipedia infobox (Chicago Defender); WTTW Chicago Tonight segment, July 11, 2019.

claims.claim: Defender weekly circulation peaked around 257,000 in 1945 and fell to 33,000 by 1970; the Pittsburgh Courier fell from 202,000 to 20,000 over the same span.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Earlier retrospectives cite a peak national circulation of about 230,000 (E&P, c.1999) — consistent in magnitude, not in year.
claims.evidence: CJR reports Defender 257,000 (1945) to 33,000 (1970); Courier 202,000 to 20,000.
claims.notes: 1945 figure matches BPM-003's verified 257,000. Brief sections: CIRCULATION, COMPARISON.
claims.source: Columbia Journalism Review, 'The Not-So-Great Migration.'

claims.claim: Circa 1999 the Defender had ABC circulation of about 13,786 weekday and 16,268 weekend and was believed to be losing money; by 2002 ABC daily circulation was about 14,629.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: E&P's 1999 piece gives ABC figures and states the paper was believed to be losing money; E&P's 2002 piece gives the 14,629 daily figure.
claims.notes: 'Believed to be losing money' is a contemporaneous reporter's judgment, not audited financials. Brief section: DECLINE.
claims.source: Editor & Publisher, 1999 ('Death Tax Claims Storied Tabloid'); Editor & Publisher, 2002 ('The Revival of the Black Press in America').

claims.claim: The Defender remained under Abbott/Sengstacke family control until the 2002-2003 Real Times LLC transaction.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: BPM-003 verifies family control through the Sengstacke era; E&P reports the bankruptcy-court-approved sale to Real Times.
claims.notes: Brief section: OWNERSHIP.
claims.source: CTL-DR-BPM-003 (verified); Editor & Publisher, 2002-2003.

claims.claim: At his death John H. Sengstacke owned 70% of Sengstacke Enterprises; his trust required a sale, and the company faced an approximately $3 million estate-tax bill.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: E&P's reporting states the 70% ownership, the trust's sale requirement, and the ~$3M estate-tax bill.
claims.notes: Brief sections: OWNERSHIP, SALE ECONOMICS.
claims.source: Editor & Publisher, 1999 ('Death Tax Claims Storied Tabloid').

claims.claim: Real Times LLC acquired the Defender in 2002-2003; reported terms were $8.5 million for 91% plus assumption of $2.4 million in debt (described as a $10.9 million deal), plus a $1.5 million technology-investment commitment.
claims.contradictory_evidence: A later E&P retrospective ('The Revival of the Black Press in America') describes the January 2003 purchase as $8.1 million — likely a different component or net-price reporting; preserve the discrepancy, do not flatten it.
claims.evidence: E&P 2002: $8.5M for 91% plus $2.4M debt assumption = $10.9M deal. E&P 2003: $1.5M technology-investment commitment.
claims.notes: Brief sections: SALE ECONOMICS.
claims.source: Editor & Publisher, 2002 ('Chicago Defender Sale OK'd'); Editor & Publisher, 2003 ('Judge OKs Sale of Chicago Defender').

claims.claim: The Defender occupied 3435 S. Indiana Avenue beginning in 1920; the exact end date of occupancy is disputed (1956 vs. 1960).
claims.confidence: high on 1920; low on end date
claims.contradictory_evidence: 1956 vs. 1960 end dates in the record.
claims.evidence: The NPS nomination documents the 1920 start; sources conflict on the end year.
claims.notes: Occupancy does not prove press ownership — do not assert pre-1960 press ownership without stronger evidence (BPM-003 caution). Brief section: INFRASTRUCTURE.
claims.source: National Park Service National Register nomination (NRHP 64000173).

claims.claim: John H. Johnson founded Johnson Publishing Company in Chicago in 1942; Ebony launched in November 1945 and the first issue's 25,000 copies sold out; circulation reached 325,000 by 1947.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: BPM-003 verifies the 1942 founding and $500-loan origin (based on Johnson's own account). Grolier Club: 25,000 first issue sold out; 325,000 by 1947.
claims.notes: Comparison case only — not Defender evidence. Brief section: COMPARISON.
claims.source: CTL-DR-BPM-003 (verified: 1942 founding, $500 loan, Negro Digest); Grolier Club exhibition catalog (25,000 first issue, 325,000 by 1947); NYPL/The HistoryMakers finding aid (corroborates $500 loan + $6,000 charter subscriptions, Negro Digest to Black World, Ebony 1945, Jet 1951).
claims.source_type: prior CTL research; institutional catalog; archival finding aid

claims.claim: Ebony circulation reached 623,000 in 1960 and passed one million in October 1967; Johnson Publishing revenue reached approximately $10 million.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None; exact year of the $10M revenue figure is not pinned.
claims.evidence: Forbes: 623,000 (1960), 1M+ (Oct 1967), ~$10M company revenue.
claims.notes: Comparison case — the strongest quantified Black-publishing consumer-advertising model. Brief section: COMPARISON.
claims.source: Forbes retrospective on Johnson (via stephenhicks.org PDF).

claims.claim: Zenith was Ebony's first major corporate advertising breakthrough; by early 1948 Ebony advertisers included Pepsi-Cola, Colgate, Beech-Nut, Seagram, and Remington Rand (Chrysler and Chesterfield also verified by BPM-003).
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: Forbes: Johnson won Zenith as the first major corporate advertiser; lists Pepsi-Cola, Colgate, Beech-Nut, Seagram, Remington Rand by early 1948. BPM-003 verifies Chrysler and Chesterfield ad examples.
claims.notes: Comparison case — do not imply the Defender had the same advertisers. Brief sections: ADVERTISING, COMPARISON.
claims.source: Forbes retrospective (Zenith breakthrough; early-1948 advertiser list); CTL-DR-BPM-003 (Chrysler, Chesterfield).

claims.claim: As migration-era Black newspaper circulation grew, northern employers and businesses placed advertising, creating a circulation/advertising feedback loop.
claims.contradictory_evidence: No primary business record (rate card, ad ledger, revenue figure) was located for the Defender itself.
claims.evidence: A secondary paper citing established scholarship describes the feedback loop.
claims.notes: Grade no higher than PROVISIONAL. This is the brief's largest advertising-side uncertainty. Brief section: ADVERTISING.
claims.source: Secondary scholarship (paper citing established migration-press scholarship).

claims.claim: An OKeh Records 'Race Record Artists Night' advertisement ran in the Chicago Defender on February 6, 1926, page 6 — primary visual evidence that entertainment/record companies bought Defender ad space targeting Black consumers.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: The preserved full-page OKeh ad from the Defender's Feb. 6, 1926 issue names Alberta Hunter and Richard M. Jones.
claims.notes: Concrete advertiser-mix evidence — the best primary ad evidence located for the Defender. Brief sections: ADVERTISING, visuals (V3).
claims.source: Surviving issue image via Wikimedia Commons (1926 issue, public domain).

claims.claim: Ebony's audited circulation fell 22% from 1.51 million (first-half 2005) to 1.18 million (first-half 2015); the 2016 sale to Clear View Group was for an undisclosed price including assumed debt; Johnson Publishing declared bankruptcy in 2019.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: Mediapost: 22% decline, undisclosed sale price with assumed debt. NPR: JPC bankruptcy 2019.
claims.notes: Comparison case for the decline mechanics of Black publishing. Brief section: COMPARISON.
claims.source: Mediapost (2016 sale coverage, audited circulation); KVNf/NPR (2019 bankruptcy).

claims.claim: The Defender's first-issue sale price was two cents per copy, with the printer extending credit.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Congressional Record (2005): a quarter each.
claims.evidence: Two sources conflict directly on the price.
claims.notes: Do not use in the brief beyond a footnote-grade dispute note, or omit. Kept in ledger for transparency.
claims.source: Educational account (unspecified in current session); contradicted by Congressional Record (2005), which says 'a quarter each.'

claims.claim: Defender printing/press costs, newsprint costs, subscription-agent and newsboy commission structures, advertiser rate cards and revenue totals, labor costs, freight costs, and daily-conversion financing are unknown from accessible evidence.
claims.confidence: UNRESOLVED (as a gap statement: VERIFIED gap)
claims.contradictory_evidence: None — but absence of access is not proof of nonexistence; records may exist in archives not yet searched (e.g., Sengstacke family papers, Chicago History Museum).
claims.evidence: BPM-003 explicitly lists distribution-agent economics, subscription volumes, advertiser mix/rates, printing costs, workforce, and plant costs as major archival gaps; this brief's sweep found no primary business records (rate cards, ledgers) for the Defender.
claims.notes: The largest structural uncertainty in the brief. Brief sections: ADVERTISING, WHAT REMAINS DISPUTED OR UNKNOWN, red-team.
claims.source: CTL-DR-BPM-003 gaps register; this brief's source sweep (2026-09-28).

claims.claim: Bud Billiken Day was founded by Abbott in 1929 and grew into the largest African-American parade in the United States (described as the second-largest parade in the country behind the Tournament of Roses).
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on founding year; 'second-largest' rankings are soft claims.
claims.evidence: Defender's 2029 coverage marks the 100th Bud Billiken Day (implying 1929 origin). Britannica describes the parade's scale.
claims.notes: Community-event economics (parade as brand asset/audience engine), not a circulation figure. Brief section: DISTRIBUTION/COMMUNITY.
claims.source: Chicago Defender coverage of the 100th Bud Billiken Day (2029); Britannica (parade ranking).

claims.claim: By the late 1910s the Defender's circulation was about 120,000, with roughly one-third in Chicago and two-thirds outside — including about 80,000 in the South.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Pre-1940 figures are publisher-claim-era numbers (BPM-003 caution).
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Chicago: circulation about 120,000; a third Chicago, two-thirds elsewhere; about 80,000 Southern.
claims.notes: National-distribution economics at its height. Brief sections: CIRCULATION, DISTRIBUTION.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago (Chicago History Museum).

claims.claim: The Defender operated largely as a Black-owned, family-controlled enterprise for nearly a century; its 2002-2003 sale was driven by estate-tax pressure after Sengstacke's death, not by a market-strategy exit.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on mechanism; do not over-claim motive — the trust's requirement is documented, deeper motives are not.
claims.evidence: E&P: trust required sale; ~$3M estate-tax bill; judge approved the Real Times deal.
claims.notes: Brief sections: OWNERSHIP, SALE ECONOMICS.
claims.source: CTL-DR-BPM-003 (family control, verified); E&P 1999-2003 (estate tax, trust requirement, court-approved sale).

claims.claim: The Defender's decline (257,000 in 1945 to 33,000 in 1970 to ~13-16,000 by 1999) parallels the broader collapse of the national Black weekly press after the civil-rights era opened mainstream papers to Black readers and advertisers.
claims.contradictory_evidence: The causal claim is an interpretation, not directly evidenced in this brief's sources.
claims.evidence: CJR and E&P provide the circulation trajectory; the structural explanation (mainstream competition for Black readers/advertisers) is the conventional scholarly account.
claims.notes: Present the trajectory as fact; the causal mechanism as interpretation with red-team flag. Brief sections: DECLINE, red-team.
claims.source: CJR (circulation series); E&P (1999, 2002).

grade_definitions.PROVISIONAL: Plausible from the evidence but thinly sourced; do not rely on without caveat.
grade_definitions.SUPPORTED: Supported by at least one credible source; not contradicted.
grade_definitions.UNRESOLVED: No usable evidence located; an archival gap.
grade_definitions.VERIFIED: Confirmed by multiple independent primary or institutional sources.

title: The Economics of the Black Newspaper
